newsitem.title: CHINA: China cannot count on long WTO transition - U.S.
newsitem.headline: China cannot count on long WTO transition - U.S.

text.p: A senior U.S. trade official said on Wednesday that China could not count on a lengthy transition in making structural economic changes to gain membership of the World Trade Organisation (WTO).

Undersecretary of Commerce Stuart Eizenstat told a business luncheon in Shanghai there was a clear understanding in the United States of the major difficulties China faced in readying its economy for membership of the WTO.
The problem of inefficient state-owned enterprises, half of which are running at a loss but which support possibly two-thirds of China's urban workforce, was particularly daunting, he said.
"That is why we talk about transition periods. But transition periods can't last 20 years," Eizenstat said.

"There has to be some commitment that at some reasonable point these enterprises are going to be operated on market principles because otherwise it's unfair to our workers and the workers in Europe and elsewhere to compete against subsidised enterprises," he added.
Beijing wants to join on the easier terms of a developing country but Washington insists the Chinese economy is too big for such treatment.
Chinese officials in Beijing on Wednesday shrugged off a U.S. suggestion that Taiwan's accession to the WTO be independent of China's, insisting that it should gain entry first.

U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky had said in Washington the United States believed Taiwan's accession to the WTO should be independent of China's and based on commercial, not political, criteria.

"Regarding WTO accession for Taiwan and the People's Republic of China, administration policy is that each accession will be judged on its own merits," Barshefsky said in a letter released to the media on Tuesday.
Asked to comment on the letter, a spokesman for the Ministry of Foreign Trade and Economic Cooperation in Beijing said: "We do not wish to see this happen. I think this will not happen."
"We reiterate... our principle that China must join the WTO before Taiwan," the spokesman said.
China, which regards Taiwan as a renegade province, has said it would accept Taiwan's membership in the WTO as a customs territory -- but only after China itself is admitted.
Taiwan is said to be much closer to meeting WTO requirements than China, which is still trying to dismantle vestiges of a centrally planned economy.
At a WTO meeting in Geneva last Friday on Taiwan's accession, trade officials said Taipei's application seemed to be unavoidably linked to Beijing's.
